notes: Extradition habeas corpus; Maurice Kay LJ's section 11(3)(b) causation analysis is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Wood v Germany: extradition habeas corpus and passage of time
key_facts: Gary Wood, a dual British-German national aged almost 18 at the time, was sought by Germany for alleged unlawful killing and GBH on New Year's Day 2002.
He was acquitted by the Regional Court of Paderborn in June 2002 but a prosecution appeal led the Federal Court to order a retrial in March 2003 after he had returned to England.
He was committed for extradition in March 2004 and applied for habeas corpus relying on delay, youth, threats from the victim's family and settled life in England.
He had previously been acquitted under German procedure allowing prosecution appeals against acquittal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for habeas corpus in the Administrative Court against extradition to Germany following committal by Bow Street Magistrates' Court.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; discharge was not required under section 11(3)(b) because the hardships relied upon were not causally linked to the passage of time.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 11(3)(b) of the Extradition Act 1989 the applicant must show that return would be unjust or oppressive by reason of the passage of time since the alleged offence; hardship, youth and changed circumstances alone do not suffice without that causal link.
legal_issues: Whether return would be unjust or oppressive under section 11(3)(b) because of delay since the alleged offences
Distinction between 'unjust' and 'oppressive' in extradition delay cases
Relevance of prior acquittal followed by ordered retrial under foreign criminal procedure
Whether threats and depressive symptoms established oppressive delay
linked_authorities: Kakis v The Government of Cyprus [1978] 1 WLR 779
Union of India v Narang [1978] AC 247

confidence.notes: Single ground, statutory test and refusal are all explicitly reasoned.

notes: Lifer Parole Board delay judicial review; Sullivan J's Article 5(4)/(5) and damages analysis is comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: Bernard v SSHD: Parole Board delay and Article 5(4)
key_facts: Bernard pleaded guilty in 1973 to the manslaughter of two 11-year-old girls and received a life sentence; his tariff expired in July 1988 but he remained in prison.
Parole Board hearings between February 2001 and September 2004 were repeatedly adjourned, largely to obtain further PPG and psychiatric evidence on sexual motivation for the index offences.
Administrative muddle by the prison service caused some delay in arranging further PPG testing after May 2002, but much delay arose from agreed adjournments and the claimant's own litigation choices.
The claimant sought declaratory relief and damages for breach of Article 5(4) and Article 5(5).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of delay in arranging a Parole Board review hearing for a discretionary life prisoner.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; no declaration against the Parole Board, limited attributable delay by the Secretary of State would not justify relief, and damages for distress were not established.
enrichment.ratio: Article 5(4) requires speedily decided reviews but permits reasonable adjournments for further evidence; isolated administrative muddle in a complex lifer case does not necessarily breach Article 5(4), and damages for frustration require significant distress proved with corroboration.
legal_issues: Whether delay between Parole Board hearings breached Article 5(4)
Attribution of delay to the Secretary of State, Parole Board or claimant
Availability of declaratory relief where errors were acknowledged but not systemic
Threshold for damages under Article 5(5) for frustration and distress
linked_authorities: R (KB and others) v South London and South and West Region Mental Health Review Tribunal [2003] EWHC 193 (Admin)
Anufrijeva v Southwark London Borough Council [2003] EWCA Civ 1406
Oldham v United Kingdom (2000)

confidence.notes: Detailed chronology and nuanced findings on attribution of delay; late distress evidence weakened damages claim.

notes: Housing benefit notification prosecution appeal; Moses LJ construes Tax Credits Act exclusion and section 116 time limits.

enrichment.short_title: Eyeson v Milton Keynes: housing benefit notification and tax credits
key_facts: Ms Eyeson was convicted of failing promptly to notify changes in Working Families' Tax Credit affecting her housing and council tax benefit.
She argued section 112(1A) did not apply because the change related to tax credit excluded by Schedule 2 paragraph 13 of the Tax Credits Act 1999.
The offences related to April and October 2002 but prosecution began after the section 116 twelve-month limit, relying on a certificate dated 23 September 2003 not put before the magistrates.
Documentary evidence sufficient to justify prosecution was available to the council by 10 February 2003.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Milton Keynes Magistrates' Court convictions for failure to notify benefit changes.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; convictions and sentence quashed because section 112(1A) applied but prosecution was out of time under section 116(2)(b).
enrichment.ratio: Schedule 2 paragraph 13 of the Tax Credits Act 1999 excludes section 112 only where the benefit or failure to notify relates to tax credit itself; a tax credit increase affecting housing benefit entitlement remains prosecutable, but section 116(2)(b) limits commencement to three months after sufficient evidence came to the authority's knowledge or twelve months from the offence.
legal_issues: Whether section 112(1A) applies where the unnotified change is an increase in Working Families' Tax Credit
Construction of 'relates to tax credit' in Schedule 2 paragraph 13
Whether prosecution was time-barred under section 116(2)(b)
Admissibility and effect of a section 116(3) certificate not before the magistrates

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and time-bar conclusions are explicit with convictions quashed.

notes: Summary contempt appeals; Hooper LJ applies Wilkinson and Griffin to deferred Crown Court contempt proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Santiago v R: summary contempt jurisdiction after trial
key_facts: During a conspiracy trial Santiago pushed a dock officer, swore and was removed from court after the jury had retired; he later refused to attend for sentencing and abused the court clerk.
Judge Findlay Baker QC found two contempts on 16 May 2003, eight days after the dock incident and after verdict and sentence in the main trial.
The appellant argued summary contempt power required immediate action and that assault should have been left to magistrates' court prosecution.
Article 6 impartiality was also raised because the trial judge dealt with the contempt himself.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against findings of contempt of court made summarily by the trial judge after conclusion of the main criminal trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeals against contempt findings dismissed; concurrent rather than consecutive sentence allowed on the second contempt.
enrichment.ratio: Urgency goes to whether summary contempt jurisdiction should be exercised, not whether it exists; a judge may defer contempt adjudication after trial where fairness permits, and refusal to obey a lawful order to attend for sentencing may constitute contempt interfering with the administration of justice.
legal_issues: Whether summary contempt could be dealt with eight days after the incident and after trial ended
Application of Balogh, Griffin, Wilkinson and Macleod to deferred contempt proceedings
Whether Article 6 required a different judge where facts were undisputed
Whether refusal to attend for sentencing constitutes contempt
index_terms: Balogh v St Albans Crown Court
linked_authorities: Balogh v St Albans Crown Court [1975] 1 QB 73
Wilkinson v S and another [2003] EWCA Civ 95
Griffin (1989) 88 Cr App R 63

notes: Landmark POCA appeal for lawyers; Court of Appeal rejects P v P on section 328 in litigation context.

enrichment.short_title: Bowman v Fels: Proceeds of Crime Act and lawyers in litigation
key_facts: Bowman claimed a constructive trust interest in a house registered in Fels's sole name after their ten-year relationship ended.
Her solicitors suspected Fels had wrongly included renovation costs in business VAT returns and disclosed suspicions to NCIS under section 328, then sought a without-notice trial adjournment.
Judge Crawford Lindsay QC vacated the trial; Judge Cowell discharged that order and refused the adjournment as improper.
The Bar Council, Law Society and NCIS intervened; the underlying dispute had settled but the court heard the appeal on public importance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Central London County Court on whether POCA obliged lawyers to suspend litigation and seek NCIS consent before continuing proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Judge Cowell's order upheld on the basis that section 328 did not require disclosure or halt ordinary conduct of legal proceedings in this context.
enrichment.ratio: Section 328 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 does not apply to require lawyers conducting litigation to disclose suspicions about opposing parties' assets derived from information obtained in the proceedings; fundamental duties to the court and client cannot be overridden without clear parliamentary intention.
legal_issues: Whether section 328 obliges solicitors to make authorised disclosures to NCIS during civil litigation
Whether lawyers must halt case preparation pending NCIS consent under section 335
Correctness of P v P (Ancillary Relief: Proceeds of Crime) on POCA in family and civil proceedings
Whether the court could hear an appeal after settlement on a point of public importance
linked_authorities: P v P (Ancillary Relief: Proceeds of Crime) [2003] EWHC 2260 (Fam)
Sun Life Assurance Co of Canada v Jervis [1944] AC 111
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex p Salem [1999] 1 AC 450

notes: Chancery amendment application; Lightman J applies Sprung and refuses loss-of-opportunity head on indemnity covenant.

enrichment.short_title: Mandrake v Countrywide: consequential loss on indemnity covenant
key_facts: Countrywide covenanted to indemnify Mandrake for pension mis-selling liabilities after selling the company to Plusnet in March 1996.
Phase 2 SIB pension review liabilities were disputed; the claimants sought declaration, rectification and account with trial listed for July 2005.
In December 2004 they sought to amend to claim £15.5 million for loss of opportunity to expand and sell Mandrake because Countrywide allegedly failed to pay indemnified liabilities promptly.
Countrywide argued the new head was bad in law following Sprung and that amendment was barred by delay and prejudice to the trial date.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Opposed application for permission to amend particulars of claim in the Chancery Division shortly before a ten-day trial window.
enrichment.outcome: Amendment refused as bad in law and on case management grounds; delay and loss of trial date weighed against granting permission.
enrichment.ratio: A claim for consequential loss arising from late payment under a contractual indemnity akin to liability insurance is not maintainable where the primary obligation is breached when the indemnified liability is incurred and damages for late payment of damages do not lie, following Sprung and The Fanti.
legal_issues: Whether loss of business expansion opportunity is recoverable for breach of an indemnity covenant
Application of Sprung v Royal Insurance to liability indemnities
Whether a first instance judge may permit a claim bound to fail to reach the Court of Appeal or House of Lords
Discretionary refusal for delay, lack of particularity and prejudice to trial date

Firma C-Trade SA v Newcastle P&I Association (The Fanti) [1991] 2 AC 35
President of India v Lips Maritime Corporation [1988] AC 395

notes: Road traffic contributory negligence appeal; Wilson LJ distinguishes Clarke v Winchurch on KEEP CLEAR junction facts.

enrichment.short_title: Fagan v Jeffers: scooter collision on KEEP CLEAR area
key_facts: Fagan's motor scooter collided with Jeffers's car on Battersea Bridge Road at the junction with Kersley Street in January 2000.
Two vans were stationary abreast in the southbound carriageway obeying a KEEP CLEAR marking; the claimant rode his scooter between the kerb and the nearside van across the marked area.
Jeffers was uninsured; damages of £37,500 were agreed and the judge apportioned liability equally.
Jeffers was turning right across the southbound lane into Kersley Street when the collision occurred in darkness.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a Central London County Court ruling finding equal contributory negligence in an uninsured motorist road traffic claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; equal apportionment of liability upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A driver crossing stationary traffic to turn into a side road must proceed with utmost care where a KEEP CLEAR area may be used by two-wheeled traffic passing on the inside; both parties undertook inherently dangerous manoeuvres and equal responsibility was appropriate.
legal_issues: Whether the defendant was negligent in crossing the KEEP CLEAR area
Standard of care when visibility is obstructed by stationary vans
Whether Clarke v Winchurch required absolution of the turning driver
Whether equal apportionment with the scooter rider was perverse
linked_authorities: Clarke v Winchurch [1969] 1 WLR 69

confidence.notes: Liability findings and apportionment reasoning are detailed and the appeal was unanimously dismissed.

notes: Fatal Accidents Act dependant appeal; Potter LJ upholds household test findings on cohabitation before death.

enrichment.short_title: Kotke v Saffarini: Fatal Accidents Act cohabitant dependant
key_facts: Trevor Snowdon was killed when Saffarini's car struck him and Linda Kotke on a Bath bridge pavement in March 2000; Kotke survived with severe injuries.
Kotke claimed loss of dependency as a dependant under section 1(3)(b), having cohabited with Snowdon but not married him.
Snowdon retained his Doncaster house as his home, electoral address and employer address until late 1999 while spending increasing time at Kotke's Sheffield home.
The judge found their centre of gravity had not shifted to a joint household until after pregnancy was discovered in mid-1998, after the two-year qualifying period began.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against a preliminary issue decision on dependant status under the Fatal Accidents Act 1976.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted but appeal dismissed; Kotke was not a dependant because she had not lived with the deceased as his wife in the same household for two years before his death.
enrichment.ratio: Section 1(3)(b) requires living together in the same household as husband and wife for at least two years before death; wanting, intending or planning to do so is distinct from actually doing so, and maintaining a separate home elsewhere may indicate the statutory threshold is not met.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'household' versus 'house' for unmarried cohabitants under section 1(3)(b)
Whether two years' cohabitation as husband and wife was established by March 1998
Relevance of retaining a separate property for work, security and negative equity
Distinction between commitment to a relationship and membership of the same household
linked_authorities: Gully v Dix [2004] EWCA Civ 139
Santos v Santos [1972] Fam 247
Pounder v London Underground Ltd [1995] PIQR P217

confidence.notes: Fact-sensitive household analysis applied correctly; appeal dismissed after full consideration of grounds.

notes: Nigerian customary marriage jurisdiction; lengthy judgment staying petitions with conditional payment under inherent jurisdiction.

enrichment.short_title: M-T v T: matrimonial jurisdiction and stay to Nigeria
key_facts: Both parties are Nigerian; the petitioner claimed customary marriages in 1993 and 2002 while the respondent denied any valid marriage.
She issued divorce petitions in England in 2003-2004; the respondent disputed jurisdiction and sought a stay in favour of Nigeria.
Maintenance pending suit orders had required the wealthy respondent to fund both sides' litigation costs during the jurisdictional dispute.
Alternative financial routes via MFPA 1984 Part III and Children Act claims remained possible if status issues were resolved abroad.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary hearing in the Family Division on jurisdiction under DMPA 1973 and whether to stay matrimonial petitions pending Nigerian proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Petitions stayed until further order with conditions including a £120,000 payment to ameliorate the petitioner's costs of pursuing her case in Nigeria; MPS orders fell away with the stay.
enrichment.ratio: Where the primary dispute concerns status and financial provision under Nigerian customary marriage law, a stay of English petitions may be appropriate; overall fairness may require a lump-sum payment under the inherent jurisdiction as a condition of stay where there is arguable marriage status and great wealth disparity.
legal_issues: Whether the court had jurisdiction based on the petitioner's habitual residence
Whether proceedings should be stayed in favour of Nigeria
Whether interim maintenance and costs orders should continue as conditions of any stay
Validity of customary marriage ceremonies under Nigerian law
linked_authorities: Mark v Mark [2004] 1 FLR 1069

confidence.notes: Core stay and conditions are clear though fact findings on customary marriage are extensive and interlocutory.

notes: Coroner Article 2 retrospectivity; Moses LJ applies McKerr to pre-HRA deaths and upholds Jamieson scope.

enrichment.short_title: Pearson v Coroner: Article 2 inquest retrospectivity
key_facts: Kelly Pearson died in November 1999 from methadone, diazepam and alcohol poisoning after wrongful arrest on an obsolete warrant and release in London.
An inquest in April 2002 returned misadventure; her mother sought a fresh inquest under section 13 for insufficiency of inquiry.
The coroner conducted a Jamieson-style inquest rather than the wider Article 2 Middleton approach because the death predated the Human Rights Act.
Middleton and Sacker had left retrospectivity open; McKerr decided Article 2 investigative duties do not apply domestically to pre-October 2000 deaths.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 13 of the Coroners Act 1988 with Attorney General fiat for a fresh inquest into a pre-HRA death.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Article 2 compliant scope was not required and even on Jamieson principles the original inquest was sufficient.
enrichment.ratio: The Article 2 procedural duty to investigate deaths is ancillary to the substantive right to life and does not apply under the Human Rights Act to deaths occurring before 2 October 2000; for such deaths 'how' the deceased came by death remains 'by what means' not broader circumstances under Jamieson.
legal_issues: Whether post-HRA inquests into pre-HRA deaths must follow Middleton Article 2 scope
Effect of In re McKerr on Middleton and Sacker
Whether the inquest was insufficient even under Jamieson
Scope of investigation into police warrant error and agencies' conduct
linked_authorities: Regina (Middleton) v West Somerset Coroner [2004] UKHL 10
Regina (Sacker) v West Yorkshire Coroner [2004] UKHL 11
In re McKerr [2004] UKHL 12
Regina v North Humberside Coroner, ex parte Jamieson [1995] QB 1
